anat-coronary.title: Coronary arteries: origin, course and territories
key: Right coronary artery: from the right (anterior) aortic sinus; left coronary artery: from the left (anterior) aortic sinus.
LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the sternocostal surface of both ventricles, the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum and the A-V bundle.
The posterior interventricular artery (PDA) runs in the posterior interventricular groove and supplies the diaphragmatic surface of both ventricles and the posterior 1/3 of the septum.
Circumflex (LCx): branches to the left atrium and to the left ventricle, including the left (obtuse) marginal artery.
Artery to the SA node: RCA 65%, circumflex 35%. Artery to the AV node: RCA 80%, circumflex 20%.

anat-dominance.title: Coronary dominance
key: Co-dominance (balanced) 70%: the right coronary has the posterior interventricular branch and the circumflex has a branch to the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle.
Right dominance (15%): the posterior interventricular artery is a large branch.
Left dominance (15%): the posterior interventricular artery is a large branch of the circumflex coronary.

anat-cardiac-veins.title: Venous drainage of the heart
key: Coronary sinus: lies between the left atrium and the diaphragmatic surface and ends in the posterior wall of the right atrium.
Tributaries of the coronary sinus: great, middle and small cardiac veins, posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium.
Anterior cardiac veins arise from the right ventricle and end in the anterior wall of the right atrium.
Venae cordis minimi drain directly into the cardiac chambers, especially on the right side.
The great cardiac vein runs with the LAD in the anterior interventricular groove; the middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery.

anat-carotid.title: Common, external and internal carotid arteries
key: Right common carotid: from the brachiocephalic artery behind the sternoclavicular joint; left common carotid: from the arch of the aorta.
The common carotid ascends in the carotid sheath, related medially to the trachea and larynx and laterally to the IJV, and ends at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-4).
The external carotid ends in the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible by dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
External carotid branches: superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, superficial temporal and maxillary.
The internal carotid has no branches in the neck; it enters the skull through the carotid canal.

key: Right subclavian: from the brachiocephalic artery behind the right sternoclavicular joint; left subclavian: from the arch of the aorta.

anat-facial-veins.title: Facial veins and the dangerous area of the face
key: Anterior facial vein: formed by the supraorbital and supratrochlear veins at the medial angle of the eye.
Retromandibular (posterior facial) vein: formed by the maxillary and superficial temporal veins inside the parotid gland; divides at the lower pole of the parotid.
Common facial vein: anterior facial vein + anterior division of the retromandibular vein; drains into the IJV.

anat-neck-veins.title: Jugular, subclavian and brachiocephalic veins
key: External jugular vein: formed by the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein; descends superficial to sternomastoid; ends in the subclavian vein.

phys-ecg-leads.title: ECG leads and what they record
key: The ECG measures the electrical activity of the heart per unit time; it does NOT measure the flow of blood through the heart.
Six limb leads (frontal plane): bipolar I, II, III and unipolar augmented aVR, aVL, aVF. Six precordial leads V1-V6 (horizontal plane).
Current flowing towards the recording electrode gives an upward deflection; current flowing away gives a downward deflection.
Views: left lateral I, aVL, V5, V6; septum V1, V2; anterior V3, V4; inferior II, III, aVF.
phys-ecg-leads.text: ecg leads and what they record the heart's electrical activity creates potential differences that the body, a good conductor, carries to the skin. each lead is a picture of that activity from one direction: limb leads in the frontal plane, chest leads in the horizontal plane. einthoven's triangle is formed by the axes of the limb leads around the heart. a nurse reassures an anxious client that the ecg only records electrical activity; it does not measure blood flow. thinking the ecg measures how well blood is pumped. it records electrical events only. bipolar = the big three (i, ii, iii); augmented = the av letters. check electrode placement before recording: wrong leads give wrong pictures. read a deflection by direction: toward the electrode = up, away = down. localize changes by lead group: inferior ii, iii, avf; lateral i, avl, v5, v6; septal v1, v2; anterior v3, v4. in a bipolar lead the potential difference is recorded between two active electrodes. leads ii, iii and avf view the inferior portion of the heart. the ecg measures the electrical activity of the heart per unit time; it does not measure the flow of blood through the heart. six limb leads (frontal plane): bipolar i, ii, iii and unipolar augmented avr, avl, avf. six precordial leads v1-v6 (horizontal plane). current flowing towards the recording electrode gives an upward deflection; current flowing away gives a downward deflection. views: left lateral i, avl, v5, v6; septum v1, v2; anterior v3, v4; inferior ii, iii, avf.

phys-sinus.title: Normal sinus rhythm and its variations
key: Normal sinus rhythm: regular, normal P waves with one P for every QRS, PR 0.12-0.20 s, normal QRS.
Sinus bradycardia: everything normal but a slow rate (35 bpm on the slide); sinus tachycardia: normal but fast (130 bpm).
Sinus arrhythmia: heart rate increases during inspiration and decreases during expiration.

phys-arrhythmia.title: Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter
key: Atrial fibrillation: no organized atrial depolarization, so no normal P waves; atrial rate usually above 350/min; irregularly irregular.
Atrial fibrillation affects 2-4%, up to 5-10% of people over 80 years old.
Atrial flutter: flutter waves instead of P waves, no measurable PR interval; rhythm regular in the slide example.

phys-av-block.title: AV nodal blocks
key: 1st degree: PR interval > 0.20 s; prolonged conduction delay in the AV node or bundle of His.
2nd degree Mobitz I: PR progressively lengthens until one impulse (usually the 3rd or 4th) fails to make it through the AV node.
2nd degree Mobitz II: occasional P waves are completely blocked with no PR prolongation (all or nothing); block typically in the bundle of His.
3rd degree: complete block in the AV junction; atria and ventricles beat independently; ventricular pacemaker at 30-45 beats/minute.
When an impulse originates in a ventricle, conduction is inefficient and the QRS is wide and bizarre.

phys-axis.title: Mean QRS axis
key: Normal ventricular depolarization flows leftward and downward because most of the ventricular mass is in the left ventricle.
Normal QRS axis: -30 to +110 degrees. Left axis deviation: -30 to -90. Right axis deviation: +110 to +180. Indeterminate (extreme right): +180 to -90.
Lead I and aVF: + + normal; + - left axis deviation; - + right axis deviation; - - right superior / indeterminate.
An abnormal axis can suggest disease such as pulmonary hypertension from a pulmonary embolism.

phys-co.title: Cardiac output, stroke volume and ejection fraction
key: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 70 x 70 = 4900 ml/min, about 5 L/min.
Stroke volume = EDV - ESV (about 70-80 ml); EDV about 120-130 ml; ESV about 50-60 ml.
EF = SV / EDV x 100; normal 50-75%, up to 90% in strenuous exercise; 30% or less in a failing heart.
Cardiac index = cardiac output per minute per square meter of body surface area; normal 3.2 L/min/m2.
Cardiac reserve = the difference between cardiac output at rest and the maximum the heart can pump per minute.
phys-co.text: cardiac output, stroke volume and ejection fraction cardiac output is how much each ventricle pumps per minute: rate times stroke volume. stroke volume is the difference between how full the ventricle gets (edv) and how much is left (esv); ejection fraction expresses it as a percentage of edv and is a good index of ventricular function. edv 125 ml, esv 50 ml: sv 75 ml, ef 75/125 x 100 = 60%. putting esv instead of sv on top of the ef fraction. ef = what left / what was there. calculate co = hr x sv and convert ml to l. calculate sv = edv - esv, then ef = sv / edv x 100. flag an ef of 30% or less as consistent with a failing heart. normal ejection fraction is about 50-75%. normal cardiac index is 3.2 l/min/m2. cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 70 x 70 = 4900 ml/min, about 5 l/min. stroke volume = edv - esv (about 70-80 ml); edv about 120-130 ml; esv about 50-60 ml. ef = sv / edv x 100; normal 50-75%, up to 90% in strenuous exercise; 30% or less in a failing heart. cardiac index = cardiac output per minute per square meter of body surface area; normal 3.2 l/min/m2. cardiac reserve = the difference between cardiac output at rest and the maximum the heart can pump per minute.

phys-autonomic.title: Autonomic control of heart rate and contractility
key: Parasympathetic (vagus) mainly supplies the atria (SA and AV nodes); parasympathetic innervation of the ventricles is sparse.
Parasympathetic: decreases heart rate, increases AV nodal delay, decreases atrial contractility, no effect on ventricular muscle.
Sympathetic: increases heart rate, decreases AV nodal delay, hastens ventricular conduction, increases atrial and ventricular contractility, promotes adrenal epinephrine.
Under resting conditions parasympathetic discharge dominates.
phys-autonomic.text: autonomic control of heart rate and contractility the vagus reaches mainly the atria (sa and av nodes), so it can slow the rate and av conduction but cannot touch ventricular contractility. sympathetic fibers reach the nodes and the ventricles, so they speed the rate and conduction and strengthen both atria and ventricles; they also release adrenal epinephrine. a frightened client's sympathetic surge raises the heart rate and ventricular contractility. giving the vagus an effect on ventricular muscle: it has none. vagus = brakes on the top floor only (atria). predict vagal effects: slower rate, longer av delay, weaker atria, ventricles unchanged. predict sympathetic effects: faster rate, shorter av delay, stronger atria and ventricles. parasympathetic stimulation increases av nodal delay. at rest, parasympathetic discharge dominates heart rate. parasympathetic (vagus) mainly supplies the atria (sa and av nodes); parasympathetic innervation of the ventricles is sparse. parasympathetic: decreases heart rate, increases av nodal delay, decreases atrial contractility, no effect on ventricular muscle. sympathetic: increases heart rate, decreases av nodal delay, hastens ventricular conduction, increases atrial and ventricular contractility, promotes adrenal epinephrine. under resting conditions parasympathetic discharge dominates.

phys-starling.title: Frank-Starling law, preload and afterload
key: Frank-Starling law: force of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fiber (EDV and stroke volume).
Resting cardiac fiber length is less than optimum, so more filling stretches fibers closer to optimum and increases the force of the next contraction.
Preload = load before contraction, the end-diastolic volume. Afterload = load the ventricle pumps against, the arterial blood pressure.
Sympathetic stimulation and epinephrine increase contractility at any EDV (more Ca2+ influx) and shift the Frank-Starling curve to the left.
phys-starling.text: frank-starling law, preload and afterload cardiac fibers at rest are shorter than their optimum length. more filling stretches them toward optimum, so the next contraction is stronger: the frank-starling law (intrinsic control). sympathetic stimulation is extrinsic: it raises contractility at any filling by increasing ca2+ influx, shifting the curve to the left. a fluid bolus raises edv and the stroke volume rises: frank-starling. calling edv afterload. pre comes before contraction (filling); after is what the ventricle pushes against. link a rise in edv (preload) to a stronger contraction through frank-starling. link sympathetic stimulation to a left shift of the curve. keep the loads apart: preload = edv; afterload = arterial pressure. the extent of filling is referred to as preload. sympathetic stimulation shifts the frank-starling curve to the left. frank-starling law: force of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fiber (edv and stroke volume). resting cardiac fiber length is less than optimum, so more filling stretches fibers closer to optimum and increases the force of the next contraction. preload = load before contraction, the end-diastolic volume. afterload = load the ventricle pumps against, the arterial blood pressure. sympathetic stimulation and epinephrine increase contractility at any edv (more ca2+ influx) and shift the frank-starling curve to the left.

phys-venous-return.title: Factors controlling venous return
key: Veins are capacitance vessels holding about 60-70% of blood; when veins store less blood, more returns to the heart.
Skeletal muscle pump: contraction compresses veins and moves blood toward the heart.
Respiratory pump: in inspiration intrathoracic pressure falls (-5 mmHg), drawing blood into the chest.
Sympathetic venoconstriction, the cardiac suction effect and one-way venous valves (every 2-4 cm) also increase venous return.
phys-venous-return.text: factors controlling venous return veins are capacitance vessels holding 60-70% of the blood. anything that squeezes them or pulls blood toward the chest moves blood back to the heart and raises edv. a client on bed rest does leg exercises; muscle contraction compresses the veins and increases venous return. thinking veins storing more blood increases return. less storage means more return. squeeze, suck, shut: muscle pump squeezes, inspiration and cardiac suction suck, valves shut backflow. encourage leg exercise (muscle pump) and deep breathing (respiratory pump) in clients on bed rest. remember sympathetic venoconstriction, cardiac suction and venous valves also help. during inspiration, intrathoracic pressure falls to about -5 mmhg. venous valves are placed at 2 to 4 cm intervals. veins are capacitance vessels holding about 60-70% of blood; when veins store less blood, more returns to the heart. skeletal muscle pump: contraction compresses veins and moves blood toward the heart. respiratory pump: in inspiration intrathoracic pressure falls (-5 mmhg), drawing blood into the chest. sympathetic venoconstriction, the cardiac suction effect and one-way venous valves (every 2-4 cm) also increase venous return.

phys-co-measure.title: Measuring cardiac output and conditions that change it
key: Fick principle: cardiac output = O2 uptake by the lungs / (arterial O2 - venous O2), e.g. 200 / (200 - 160) = 5 L/min.
Cardiac output rises in hyperthyroidism, anemia and fever; falls in hypothyroidism, myocardial damage and failure, valvular disease, arrhythmias, hemorrhage and shock.
Most common causes of heart failure: myocardial infarction, then working against increased afterload (hypertension, aortic stenosis).
phys-co-measure.text: measuring cardiac output and conditions that change it the fick principle says the oxygen the lungs take up equals blood flow times the oxygen each liter picks up. so flow (cardiac output) = o2 uptake / arterial-venous o2 difference, with venous blood taken from the pulmonary artery. o2 uptake 250 ml/min, a-v difference 50 ml/l: cardiac output 5 l/min. dividing by arterial o2 content instead of the a-v difference. fick: flow = uptake / difference. set up fick: o2 uptake (ml/min) / (arterial - venous o2, ml/l). recognize conditions that raise co (hyperthyroidism, anemia, fever) and lower it (hypothyroidism, failure, valve disease, arrhythmias, hemorrhage). cardiac output can also be measured by dye dilution and doppler combined with echocardiography. fick principle: cardiac output = o2 uptake by the lungs / (arterial o2 - venous o2), e.g. 200 / (200 - 160) = 5 l/min. cardiac output rises in hyperthyroidism, anemia and fever; falls in hypothyroidism, myocardial damage and failure, valvular disease, arrhythmias, hemorrhage and shock. most common causes of heart failure: myocardial infarction, then working against increased afterload (hypertension, aortic stenosis).

phys-coronary-flow.title: Coronary blood flow and oxygen extraction
key: Coronary blood flow at rest is about 225-250 ml/minute, about 5% of cardiac output.
At rest the heart extracts 60-70% of the oxygen from each unit of blood (other tissues about 25%).
Up to 40% of the cardiac cell is mitochondria, so the heart needs more O2; when more O2 is needed, delivery rises only by increasing blood flow.
The heart uses mainly free fatty acids; in ischemia it uses anaerobic glycolysis, forming lactic acid (one cause of cardiac pain).
phys-coronary-flow.text: coronary blood flow and oxygen extraction cardiac muscle is packed with mitochondria and works aerobically, so it already takes 60-70% of the oxygen it receives. with so little left to extract, more oxygen can reach it only by more flow. a client with coronary disease starts exercising; the heart can meet the extra demand only by increasing coronary flow. thinking the heart can extract much more oxygen when needed, like other tissues. heart takes two thirds already; it needs more flow, not more extraction. expect symptoms when demand rises and flow cannot: angina on effort. link ischemic pain to lactic acid from anaerobic glycolysis. at rest the heart extracts 60-70% of oxygen; other tissues extract about 25%. coronary blood flow at rest is about 225-250 ml/minute, about 5% of cardiac output. at rest the heart extracts 60-70% of the oxygen from each unit of blood (other tissues about 25%). up to 40% of the cardiac cell is mitochondria, so the heart needs more o2; when more o2 is needed, delivery rises only by increasing blood flow. the heart uses mainly free fatty acids; in ischemia it uses anaerobic glycolysis, forming lactic acid (one cause of cardiac pain).

phys-phasic-flow.title: Phasic changes in coronary flow
key: Left ventricular flow falls in systole: the contracting LV compresses the coronary arteries and the open aortic valve partially blocks their entrance.
Systole: aorta 120, LV 121 mmHg (gradient -1); diastole: aorta 80, LV 0 (gradient 80). Right ventricle gradient is 95 in systole, 80 in diastole.
The subendocardial surface of the left ventricle gets almost no flow in systole, so it is the most common site of myocardial infarction.
Tachycardia shortens diastole and reduces coronary flow; aortic stenosis and low aortic diastolic pressure also reduce LV flow.
phys-phasic-flow.text: phasic changes in coronary flow the left ventricle squeezes its own coronary vessels in systole and the open aortic valve partly covers their openings, so left ventricular flow happens mainly in diastole. the right ventricle's lower pressure leaves a large aorta-rv gradient in systole, so its flow is preserved. a client with a rate of 150 complains of chest tightness: shortened diastole reduces coronary flow. thinking a faster rate improves coronary flow. the left heart feeds itself between beats. treat tachycardia as a threat to coronary flow because diastole shortens. expect the lv subendocardium to be hit first in ischemia. remember aortic stenosis and low aortic diastolic pressure reduce lv flow. in systole the aorta-to-left-ventricle pressure gradient is about -1 mmhg. the most common site of myocardial infarction is the subendocardial layer of the left ventricle. left ventricular flow falls in systole: the contracting lv compresses the coronary arteries and the open aortic valve partially blocks their entrance. systole: aorta 120, lv 121 mmhg (gradient -1); diastole: aorta 80, lv 0 (gradient 80). right ventricle gradient is 95 in systole, 80 in diastole. the subendocardial surface of the left ventricle gets almost no flow in systole, so it is the most common site of myocardial infarction. tachycardia shortens diastole and reduces coronary flow; aortic stenosis and low aortic diastolic pressure also reduce lv flow.

phys-coronary-control.title: Chemical and neural control of coronary flow
key: Coronary blood flow shows considerable autoregulation.
Vasodilators: lack of oxygen, increased CO2, H+, K+, lactate, prostaglandins, adenosine and adenine nucleotides.
Adenosine, formed from ATP during cardiac metabolic activity, causes coronary vasodilatation.

Direct sympathetic effect: alpha-receptor vasoconstriction (seen when beta receptors are blocked). Indirect effect in the intact body: beta-1 raises heart rate and contractility, releasing vasodilator metabolites.
Parasympathetic influences are minor and weakly vasodilatory.
phys-coronary-control.text: chemical and neural control of coronary flow coronary flow follows metabolism: working muscle produces co2, h+, k+, lactate, adenosine and other metabolites, and lack of oxygen itself dilates the vessels. sympathetic nerves act two ways: directly they constrict (alpha), but indirectly, by making the heart work harder (beta-1), they release dilating metabolites, which wins in the intact body. in shock, reflex sympathetic discharge raises coronary flow through metabolic changes while other organs are compromised. assuming the direct sympathetic effect on coronaries is dilation. directly: constrict. indirectly: increase work, increase flow. expect coronary dilation in hypoxia and with local metabolites (adenosine). explain that beta blockade unmasks the direct constrictor effect of norepinephrine. adenosine is formed from atp during cardiac metabolic activity. parasympathetic influences on coronary vessels are minor and weakly vasodilatory. coronary blood flow shows considerable autoregulation. vasodilators: lack of oxygen, increased co2, h+, k+, lactate, prostaglandins, adenosine and adenine nucleotides. adenosine, formed from atp during cardiac metabolic activity, causes coronary vasodilatation. direct sympathetic effect: alpha-receptor vasoconstriction (seen when beta receptors are blocked). indirect effect in the intact body: beta-1 raises heart rate and contractility, releasing vasodilator metabolites. parasympathetic influences are minor and weakly vasodilatory.

phys-ihd.title: Ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction
key: Risk factors of IHD: cigarette smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, increased lipids (cholesterol), lack of exercise, anxiety.
Angina: retrosternal tightness or pain for a few minutes, often radiating to the inner side of the left arm, precipitated by effort and relieved by rest.
MI: at least 75% of the coronary lumen blocked by thrombus.
ECG: ST depression in IHD; ST elevation in MI, in the respective leads.
Treatment: coronary dilators (nitrates), beta-blockers, angioplasty, stent, bypass surgery.
phys-ihd.text: ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction atherosclerotic plaque narrows the coronary lumen. when demand rises, flow cannot keep up and the client gets angina; when a thrombus blocks at least 75% of the lumen, myocardium dies (mi). the ecg separates them: st depression in ischemia, st elevation in infarction. an exercise test shows horizontal st depression: ischemic heart disease. mixing up st depression (angina) and st elevation (mi). elevation = emergency (infarct); depression = demand ischemia. ask about effort-related retrosternal pain relieved by rest. report st elevation in a client with chest pain as consistent with mi. expect investigations: ecg, cardiac enzymes (ck, ldh, troponin), echo, treadmill, thallium, angiography. treatment of ihd includes coronary dilators such as nitrates, beta-blockers, angioplasty, stents and bypass surgery. risk factors of ihd: cigarette smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, increased lipids (cholesterol), lack of exercise, anxiety. angina: retrosternal tightness or pain for a few minutes, often radiating to the inner side of the left arm, precipitated by effort and relieved by rest. mi: at least 75% of the coronary lumen blocked by thrombus. ecg: st depression in ihd; st elevation in mi, in the respective leads. treatment: coronary dilators (nitrates), beta-blockers, angioplasty, stent, bypass surgery.

path-congestion.title: Hyperemia and congestion
key: Hyperemia: an active process in which arteriolar dilation increases blood flow; tissue turns red (erythema) from oxygenated blood.
Congestion: a passive process from impaired venous outflow; tissue is dusky reddish-blue (cyanosis) from deoxygenated blood.
Acute localized congestion: sudden complete venous obstruction (DVT, ligature, twisted pedicle of an ovary) causing rapid edema and hemorrhage.
Chronic generalized venous congestion is caused by chronic right-sided heart failure; acute generalized congestion by acute heart failure.
path-congestion.text: hyperemia and congestion both hyperemia and congestion mean more blood in a tissue, with dilated capillaries and a risk of edema. the difference is the direction of the problem: hyperemia is active arterial inflow (red, oxygenated), congestion is passive venous outflow failure (blue, deoxygenated). chronic left failure or mitral stenosis congests the lungs, producing heart failure cells and brown induration. a client with a dvt has a dusky reddish-blue swollen leg: acute localized congestion. calling the red face of exercise or blushing congestion; it is hyperemia. hyperemia is hot and red (active); congestion is clogged and blue (passive). use color to tell them apart: red = hyperemia, dusky blue = congestion. link chronic right-sided failure to generalized congestion and cardiac edema. link chronic left-sided failure and mitral stenosis to pulmonary congestion. hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages are called heart failure cells. long-standing pulmonary congestion with fibrosis causes brown induration of the lung. hyperemia: an active process in which arteriolar dilation increases blood flow; tissue turns red (erythema) from oxygenated blood. congestion: a passive process from impaired venous outflow; tissue is dusky reddish-blue (cyanosis) from deoxygenated blood. acute localized congestion: sudden complete venous obstruction (dvt, ligature, twisted pedicle of an ovary) causing rapid edema and hemorrhage. chronic generalized venous congestion is caused by chronic right-sided heart failure; acute generalized congestion by acute heart failure.

path-edema.title: Edema: causes and classification
key: Edema: an abnormal increase in interstitial fluid within tissues; fluid may be transudate, exudate or lymph.
Causes: increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, lymphatic obstruction.
Hypoproteinemia: total plasma proteins below 2.5 gm% or serum albumin below 1.5 gm%.
Pitting edema: generalized edema and obstructive venous edema. Non-pitting: inflammatory and lymphatic edema.
path-edema.text: edema: causes and classification fluid leaves capillaries when the pushing force rises (hydrostatic pressure), the holding force falls (colloid osmotic pressure), the wall leaks (permeability) or the drain is blocked (lymphatics). edema fluid may be a transudate, an exudate or lymph. a malnourished client with serum albumin below 1.5 gm% develops nutritional edema from low colloid osmotic pressure. expecting lymphatic edema (e.g. filariasis) to pit. four ways to flood: push up, pull down, leak, block. match the cause to the mechanism before choosing a treatment focus. press the skin: pitting suggests generalized or venous edema; non-pitting suggests inflammatory or lymphatic edema. fluid in the pleural cavity is called hydrothorax. generalized edema due to renal failure is called renal edema. edema: an abnormal increase in interstitial fluid within tissues; fluid may be transudate, exudate or lymph. causes: increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, lymphatic obstruction. hypoproteinemia: total plasma proteins below 2.5 gm% or serum albumin below 1.5 gm%. pitting edema: generalized edema and obstructive venous edema. non-pitting: inflammatory and lymphatic edema.

path-ischemia-infarct.title: Ischemia and infarction
key: Ischemia: deficient arterial blood supply due to partial or complete occlusion of the artery; acute (sudden complete) or chronic (gradual partial).
Organs with good collateral circulation show no effect; poor collateral circulation leads to infarction (acute) or chronic ischemic changes.
Infarct: an area of ischemic necrosis from occlusion of the arterial supply or venous drainage; 99% from thrombosis or embolism.
Red infarct: venous occlusion (ovary), loose tissue (lung), dual circulation (lung, liver, small intestine), reperfusion after angioplasty.
White infarct: arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation (heart, spleen, kidney); tissue density limits seepage of blood.
path-ischemia-infarct.text: ischemia and infarction ischemia is too little arterial supply. whether it kills tissue depends on speed and collaterals: sudden complete occlusion in an organ with poor collaterals gives an infarct. infarct color depends on whether blood can seep in: loose tissue, dual supply, venous occlusion or reperfusion give red infarcts; dense end-arterial organs give white ones. after angioplasty restores flow to an infarcted area, the infarct turns red (reperfusion). calling a lung infarct white. solid organs, end arteries, white (heart, spleen, kidney). predict red vs white from the organ: lung, liver, intestine, ovary red; heart, spleen, kidney white. think venous infarction in organs with a single venous outflow (testis, ovary). about 99% of infarcts result from thrombosis or embolism. infarcts are also classified as septic or bland (aseptic). ischemia: deficient arterial blood supply due to partial or complete occlusion of the artery; acute (sudden complete) or chronic (gradual partial). organs with good collateral circulation show no effect; poor collateral circulation leads to infarction (acute) or chronic ischemic changes. infarct: an area of ischemic necrosis from occlusion of the arterial supply or venous drainage; 99% from thrombosis or embolism. red infarct: venous occlusion (ovary), loose tissue (lung), dual circulation (lung, liver, small intestine), reperfusion after angioplasty. white infarct: arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation (heart, spleen, kidney); tissue density limits seepage of blood.

path-virchow.title: Thrombosis and Virchow's triad
key: Thrombosis: formation of a compact mass of circulating blood elements inside the cardiovascular system during life.
Virchow's triad: endothelial injury/dysfunction, alterations in blood flow (stasis or turbulence), hypercoagulability.
Endothelial dysfunction increases procoagulants (thromboplastin, vWF, PAI) and decreases anticoagulants (thrombomodulin, antithrombin III, NO, PA).
Stasis reduces inflow of fresh blood containing natural anticoagulants and retards removal of small platelet aggregates.

Acquired hypercoagulability: prolonged bed rest, surgery, burns, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, disseminated cancer, smoking, DIC. Hereditary: factor V and prothrombin gene mutations, antithrombin III deficiency.
path-virchow.text: thrombosis and virchow's triad hemostasis depends on the vessel wall, platelets and coagulation factors. virchow's triad names the three ways it tips into thrombosis: damaged or dysfunctional endothelium, abnormal flow (stasis or turbulence), and blood that clots too easily. a postoperative client on bed rest has stasis and acquired hypercoagulability: two arms of the triad. listing edema mechanisms (permeability, lymphatic obstruction) as causes of thrombosis. virchow = vessel wall, velocity (flow), viscosity-like clotting (hypercoagulability). screen surgical and immobile clients for all three triad factors. separate hereditary (factor v, prothrombin gene, antithrombin iii deficiency) from acquired hypercoagulability. turbulence mechanically injures endothelial cells. dic is an acquired cause of hypercoagulability. thrombosis: formation of a compact mass of circulating blood elements inside the cardiovascular system during life. virchow's triad: endothelial injury/dysfunction, alterations in blood flow (stasis or turbulence), hypercoagulability. endothelial dysfunction increases procoagulants (thromboplastin, vwf, pai) and decreases anticoagulants (thrombomodulin, antithrombin iii, no, pa). stasis reduces inflow of fresh blood containing natural anticoagulants and retards removal of small platelet aggregates. acquired hypercoagulability: prolonged bed rest, surgery, burns, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, disseminated cancer, smoking, dic. hereditary: factor v and prothrombin gene mutations, antithrombin iii deficiency.

path-thrombus-types.title: Sites, types and fate of thrombi
key: Venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis, red thrombi) are the most common type, associated with stasis and hypercoagulability.
DVT sites: popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; complication: embolism to the lungs (pulmonary infarction).
Arterial thrombosis is less common because of rapid flow and the thick elastic arterial wall; most common cause is atherosclerosis (coronary, cerebral, femoral).
Cardiac thrombi: auricular thrombus in the left atrium in mitral stenosis; mural thrombus in the left ventricle over an infarct; vegetations on valves.
Fate: dissolution, propagation (a tail liable to detach), embolization, organization and recanalization.
path-thrombus-types.text: sites, types and fate of thrombi where a thrombus forms depends on local conditions: slow venous flow plus hypercoagulability gives venous (red) thrombi; atherosclerotic arteries give arterial thrombi; stasis in a dilated atrium or over an infarct gives cardiac thrombi. once formed, a thrombus can dissolve, grow, break off or be organized. a client with mitral stenosis develops an auricular thrombus in the left atrium. thinking arterial thrombi are most common. venous thrombi are. veins: slow and sticky; arteries: fast and thick-walled. monitor a client with dvt for pulmonary embolism. watch for propagation: a tail makes detachment more likely. thrombi of infected veins are called thrombophlebitis. septic thrombi that embolize produce pyemia. venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis, red thrombi) are the most common type, associated with stasis and hypercoagulability. dvt sites: popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; complication: embolism to the lungs (pulmonary infarction). arterial thrombosis is less common because of rapid flow and the thick elastic arterial wall; most common cause is atherosclerosis (coronary, cerebral, femoral). cardiac thrombi: auricular thrombus in the left atrium in mitral stenosis; mural thrombus in the left ventricle over an infarct; vegetations on valves. fate: dissolution, propagation (a tail liable to detach), embolization, organization and recanalization.

path-embolism.title: Embolism and pulmonary embolism
key: An embolus is a detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass carried by the blood to a site distant from its origin.
Thromboemboli are the most common type (99%); others: fat, parasitic, air or nitrogen, amniotic fluid, tumor, cholesterol and foreign body emboli.
Pulmonary emboli: 95% originate from deep vein thrombi of the legs; seen in up to 25-30% of DVT patients; 60-80% are small and silent.

Saddle embolus causes sudden death (acute right failure); medium emboli give hemorrhage in a normal lung or infarction in a congested lung; small repeated emboli give pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
path-embolism.text: embolism and pulmonary embolism an embolus is anything solid, liquid or gas carried away from where it formed. almost all are thromboemboli, and almost all pulmonary emboli come from leg dvt. what happens next depends on embolus size and the state of the lung. a client with heart failure and lung congestion gets a medium embolus: pulmonary infarction. expecting a medium embolus in a healthy lung to infarct; it causes hemorrhage only. big = dead, medium = depends on the lung, small and many = pulmonary hypertension. suspect pe in a postoperative or immobile client with sudden dyspnea. expect a saddle embolus to cause sudden death from acute right-sided failure. about 60-80% of pulmonary emboli are small and clinically silent. an embolus is a detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass carried by the blood to a site distant from its origin. thromboemboli are the most common type (99%); others: fat, parasitic, air or nitrogen, amniotic fluid, tumor, cholesterol and foreign body emboli. pulmonary emboli: 95% originate from deep vein thrombi of the legs; seen in up to 25-30% of dvt patients; 60-80% are small and silent. saddle embolus causes sudden death (acute right failure); medium emboli give hemorrhage in a normal lung or infarction in a congested lung; small repeated emboli give pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

path-systemic-emboli.title: Systemic, fat, air and amniotic fluid emboli
key: Systemic emboli: 80% from intracardiac thrombi (2/3 left ventricular wall infarcts, 1/3 dilated left atria or vegetations); also aortic aneurysm, ulcerated plaques, paradoxical emboli.
Paradoxical emboli start as venous emboli but pass through an interatrial or interventricular defect into the systemic circulation.
Site of arrest: 75% lower extremities, 10% brain.
Fat embolism: long bone fracture is the most common cause; the syndrome begins 1-3 days after injury with tachypnea, dyspnea, tachycardia, neurologic symptoms, thrombocytopenia and anemia.
Air embolism needs more than 100 cc of air for a pulmonary effect; causes include neck vein injury, chest wall injury, obstetric or laparoscopic procedures, bypass surgery and decompression sickness.
Amniotic fluid embolism: 1 in 40,000 deliveries, mortality 80%; sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, shock, seizures, pulmonary edema and DIC.

path-arf.title: Acute rheumatic fever: pathogenesis and lesions
key: ARF is an acute, immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease a few weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
It appears 10 days to 6 weeks after pharyngitis, in about 3% of infected patients, most often in children aged 5-15.
Antibodies and CD4+ T cells against streptococcal M proteins cross-react with self antigens in the heart.
Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic: focal necrosis, T lymphocytes and Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells with a slender wavy ribbon of chromatin.
Pancarditis: fibrinous "bread and butter" pericarditis, myocarditis, and small vegetations along the lines of closure over fibrinoid necrosis (mitral 65%, aortic 25%).
path-arf.text: acute rheumatic fever: pathogenesis and lesions weeks after strep throat, antibodies and t cells made against streptococcal m proteins cross-react with heart antigens. complement and macrophages are activated and aschoff bodies form in every layer of the heart, giving pancarditis. a 14-year-old with a sore throat 3 weeks ago, fever, nodules and a new apical murmur: biopsy shows fibrinoid necrosis with histiocytes. thinking the streptococcus infects the heart directly; the damage is immune cross-reaction. m protein mimics heart. ask about a sore throat 10 days to 6 weeks before. recognize aschoff bodies and anitschkow cells as pathognomonic. prompt antibiotic treatment of strep pharyngitis prevents disease. anitschkow cells are also called caterpillar cells. rheumatic vegetations overlie foci of fibrinoid necrosis. arf is an acute, immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease a few weeks after group a streptococcal pharyngitis. it appears 10 days to 6 weeks after pharyngitis, in about 3% of infected patients, most often in children aged 5-15. antibodies and cd4+ t cells against streptococcal m proteins cross-react with self antigens in the heart. aschoff bodies are pathognomonic: focal necrosis, t lymphocytes and anitschkow (caterpillar) cells with a slender wavy ribbon of chromatin. pancarditis: fibrinous "bread and butter" pericarditis, myocarditis, and small vegetations along the lines of closure over fibrinoid necrosis (mitral 65%, aortic 25%).

path-jones.title: Jones criteria
key: Major: carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Minor: fever, arthralgia, previous rheumatic fever, raised ESR, CRP or leukocytosis, prolonged PR interval.
Evidence of preceding group A strep: positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or raised or rising streptococcal antibody titer.
Diagnosis: 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, supported by evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection.
Migratory polyarthritis of large joints is self-limited with no chronic deformities.

path-rhd.title: Chronic rheumatic heart disease and mitral stenosis
key: Endocarditis of ARF heals by fibrosis; repeated pharyngeal infections reactivate the disease and scar the valves.
Mitral valve most commonly affected, then aortic; fibrosis of the leaflets leads to stenosis ("fish mouth" or "buttonhole").
Usually becomes clinically manifest decades after ARF.

Mitral stenosis: left atrial dilatation (with thrombi), chronic pulmonary venous congestion, lung fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, chronic right-sided failure; the left ventricle is largely unaffected.
Other complications: arrhythmias (especially atrial fibrillation), thromboembolism, infective endocarditis.

path-arteriosclerosis.title: Arteriosclerosis patterns

Mönckeberg medial sclerosis: calcific deposits in muscular arteries in people older than 50.
Arteriolosclerosis: small arteries and arterioles, with hypertension and diabetes; hyaline (amorphous proteinaceous wall) and hyperplastic ("onion-skinning").

path-athero.title: Atherosclerosis: risk factors, pathogenesis and plaque
key: Atherosclerosis: a chronic inflammatory disease of the arterial wall with intimal atheromas that protrude into the lumen and weaken the media.
Non-modifiable risk factors: increasing age, male gender, family history. Modifiable: hyperlipidemia (LDL), hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus.

Response to injury: chronic endothelial injury, endothelial dysfunction with monocyte adhesion, smooth muscle recruitment and macrophage activation, foam cells, then smooth muscle proliferation and collagen deposition.
Fatty spots (<1 mm, foam cells) are the earliest lesion; fatty streaks (1 cm or longer) are not significantly raised and do not disturb blood flow.
Atheroma: raised intimal patch with a soft yellow lipid core under a firm white fibrous cap; cells, ECM and lipid.

key: Common sites: lower abdominal aorta, coronary, popliteal and internal carotid arteries, and the circle of Willis.
Acute plaque changes: rupture, ulceration or erosion (induces thrombosis), and fissure with hemorrhage into the plaque.
Other complications: atheroembolism, aneurysm from weakened media, calcification.
Consequences: ischemic heart disease (coronary), stroke (cerebral), aortic aneurysm (aorta), peripheral vascular disease with gangrene (leg arteries).

pharm-classes.title: Hypertension: definition and drug classes
key: Hypertension is defined as 130/80 mm Hg or higher (ACC/AHA 2023 and Saudi Heart Association).
Classes: diuretics, calcium channel blockers, drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system, sympatholytic drugs, vasodilators.

pharm-diuretics.title: Diuretics in hypertension
key: Early: diuretics lower plasma volume and cardiac output. After 4-8 weeks volume and output return toward normal while peripheral vascular resistance falls (arteriolar vasodilation).
Main mechanism of the vasodilation: depletion of body Na+, lowering smooth muscle Na+ and then intracellular Ca++ via the Na/Ca exchanger.
Thiazides are first choice; antihypertensive doses are lower than diuretic doses.
Loop diuretics are preferable in malignant hypertension and chronic kidney disease.
Potassium-sparing diuretics are used with thiazides to counteract hypokalemia; spironolactone is used in hyperaldosteronism.

key: CCBs bind the L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channel from the inner side of the membrane.

First-choice drugs, more effective in African patients; nicardipine for hypertensive emergencies; short-acting nifedipine increases mortality.

key: Aliskiren competitively inhibits renin: angiotensin I, II and aldosterone fall and renin rises; hyperkalemia when combined with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to II and raise bradykinin; less angiotensin II removes negative feedback, so renin rises.

pharm-alpha-beta.title: Alpha blockers, beta blockers and alpha-beta blockers

pharm-vasodilators.title: Direct vasodilators
key: Nitroprusside: arterioles and veins, nitric oxide; metabolized by red cells releasing cyanide (to thiocyanate); half-life about 2 minutes, continuous infusion; for emergencies, severe heart failure, controlled hypotension.

key: Total blood cholesterol comes from diet and endogenous synthesis and is carried by lipoproteins, especially LDL and HDL.

bio-fats.title: Types of dietary fat and their effects
key: Saturated fats (no double bonds; dairy, meat, coconut and palm oils) raise TC and LDL-C and CHD risk.
Monounsaturated fats (one double bond; olive oil, oleic acid, omega-9) lower TC and LDL-C and raise HDL-C when substituted for saturated fats.
Omega-6 fats (first double bond at carbon 6 from the methyl end; corn, sesame, cottonseed, sunflower oils) lower TC and LDL-C but also lower HDL-C and are proinflammatory.
Omega-3 fats suppress arrhythmia, reduce blood triacylglycerol, decrease thrombosis and inflammation, with little effect on LDL-C and HDL-C.
Trans fats are chemically unsaturated but behave like saturated fats: they raise LDL-C and lower HDL-C; formed by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (margarine).

bio-ros.title: Free radicals, ROS and RNS
key: Oxidative stress: an imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants, potentially leading to damage.
A free radical is a molecule with an unpaired electron in an outer valence shell; it plucks an electron from the nearest molecule.
ROS radicals: superoxide, hydroxyl, peroxyl. ROS non-radicals: hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid, ozone.
RNS radicals: nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide. RNS non-radical: peroxynitrite.

Endogenous sources: electron leak from the respiratory chain, oxidases (xanthine oxidase), prostaglandin synthesis, NO from arginine, phagocytosis. Exogenous: drug metabolism (halothane, cytochrome P450), ionizing radiation, cigarette smoke.

micro-ie-types.title: Infective endocarditis: classification and organisms
key: IE: infection of the endocardium and its valves (native or prosthetic) with septic vegetations; left-sided in over 95% of cases.
Acute IE: rapid (hours to days), mostly healthy valves, severe symptoms; S. aureus, S. pyogenes; mitral and aortic valves.
Subacute IE: slow (weeks to months), preexisting valve disease, low-grade fever, weight loss; viridans streptococci, enterococci, HACEK.
Prosthetic valve IE: early (within 12 months, intraoperative contamination) or late; mostly S. epidermidis and S. aureus.
IV drug use IE: mainly the tricuspid valve; S. aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Candida.
micro-ie-types.text: infective endocarditis: classification and organisms infective endocarditis is classified by speed (acute vs subacute), by the valve (native, prosthetic, device) and by the route (iv drug use). virulent organisms attack healthy valves fast; less virulent ones need a damaged valve and take weeks. a client who injects drugs has tricuspid vegetations and gram-positive cocci in clusters: s. aureus. assuming subacute ie affects healthy valves. acute = aureus, aggressive; subacute = slow, strep viridans. match setting to organism: iv drug use = tricuspid, s. aureus; prosthetic valve = s. epidermidis or s. aureus; damaged valve after dental work = viridans. left-sided endocarditis accounts for more than 95% of cases. early prosthetic valve endocarditis develops within 12 months of surgery. ie: infection of the endocardium and its valves (native or prosthetic) with septic vegetations; left-sided in over 95% of cases. acute ie: rapid (hours to days), mostly healthy valves, severe symptoms; s. aureus, s. pyogenes; mitral and aortic valves. subacute ie: slow (weeks to months), preexisting valve disease, low-grade fever, weight loss; viridans streptococci, enterococci, hacek. prosthetic valve ie: early (within 12 months, intraoperative contamination) or late; mostly s. epidermidis and s. aureus. iv drug use ie: mainly the tricuspid valve; s. aureus, pseudomonas aeruginosa, candida.

micro-organisms.title: Specific organisms and their associations
key: S. aureus: most common overall, IV drug users and healthcare-associated IE; acute, rapid valve destruction.
Streptococcus bovis is associated with colorectal carcinoma or GI lesions.
Enterococcus faecalis: elderly and hospital-acquired IE, after genitourinary or gastrointestinal procedures.

HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, Kingella): slow-growing fastidious Gram-negative bacilli of pharyngeal flora; subacute IE with negative cultures unless special media are used.
Cardiac device IE (pacemaker, ICD) usually comes from skin contamination at implantation; mostly staphylococci.
micro-organisms.text: specific organisms and their associations each organism hints at its source: skin and devices (staphylococci), mouth (viridans), bowel (s. bovis), urinary or gi tract (enterococci), pharynx (hacek). an elderly client gets endocarditis after a urinary procedure: enterococcus faecalis. thinking the k in hacek is klebsiella (it is kingella). hacek = haemophilus, aggregatibacter, cardiobacterium, eikenella, kingella. after s. bovis endocarditis, expect evaluation of the colon. think hacek when cultures stay negative without special media. streptococcus bovis is associated with colorectal carcinoma. s. aureus: most common overall, iv drug users and healthcare-associated ie; acute, rapid valve destruction. streptococcus bovis is associated with colorectal carcinoma or gi lesions. enterococcus faecalis: elderly and hospital-acquired ie, after genitourinary or gastrointestinal procedures. hacek (haemophilus, aggregatibacter, cardiobacterium hominis, eikenella corrodens, kingella): slow-growing fastidious gram-negative bacilli of pharyngeal flora; subacute ie with negative cultures unless special media are used. cardiac device ie (pacemaker, icd) usually comes from skin contamination at implantation; mostly staphylococci.

micro-patho.title: Pathophysiology of infective endocarditis
key: IE needs endothelial injury, bacteremia and microbial adherence leading to vegetation formation.
Damaged valvular endothelium collects platelets and fibrin, forming a sterile microthrombus (sterile vegetation).
Adherence factors: S. aureus clumping factor and fibronectin-binding protein; viridans streptococci dextran; E. faecalis teichoic acid; Gram-negatives pili.
Vegetations contain fibrin, platelets, bacteria and inflammatory cells; they are friable and embolize, and the bacteria are protected from phagocytes and antibiotics.
Consequences: valve destruction with regurgitation and heart failure, septic emboli with infarcts or abscesses, immune complex glomerulonephritis and vasculitis.
micro-patho.text: pathophysiology of infective endocarditis three things must meet: a damaged valve surface with a sterile platelet-fibrin clot, bacteria in the blood, and bacteria able to stick. inside the vegetation bacteria hide from phagocytes and antibiotics, shed into the blood and break off as emboli. a client with valve disease develops a vegetation after a dental procedure. thinking antibiotics reach organisms in vegetations easily. injury, bacteremia, adherence, vegetation. ask about recent dental, skin or invasive procedures (transient bacteremia). watch for embolic infarcts and abscesses in brain, kidney, spleen and lung. viridans streptococci adhere using dextran. immune complex deposition can cause glomerulonephritis. ie needs endothelial injury, bacteremia and microbial adherence leading to vegetation formation. damaged valvular endothelium collects platelets and fibrin, forming a sterile microthrombus (sterile vegetation). adherence factors: s. aureus clumping factor and fibronectin-binding protein; viridans streptococci dextran; e. faecalis teichoic acid; gram-negatives pili. vegetations contain fibrin, platelets, bacteria and inflammatory cells; they are friable and embolize, and the bacteria are protected from phagocytes and antibiotics. consequences: valve destruction with regurgitation and heart failure, septic emboli with infarcts or abscesses, immune complex glomerulonephritis and vasculitis.

micro-signs.title: Clinical features of infective endocarditis
key: Acute: high fever and sepsis. Subacute: mild fever, headache, myalgia, weight loss, night sweats. Cardiac: murmur, heart failure.
Splinter hemorrhages: petechial hemorrhages under the fingernails.
Janeway lesions: small, nontender, erythematous lesions on palms and soles. Osler nodes: painful nodules on the pads of fingers and toes.
Roth spots: retinal hemorrhages.
micro-signs.text: clinical features of infective endocarditis the extracardiac signs come from septic emboli and immune-mediated injury: small hemorrhages and lesions in nails, skin and retina. a client has painful nodules on the finger pads: osler nodes. mixing up janeway (painless) and osler (painful). osler = ouch; janeway = painless palms. inspect nails, palms, soles, finger pads and retina in suspected ie. separate ie signs from rheumatic fever signs (erythema marginatum, extensor nodules, chorea). roth spots are retinal hemorrhages. acute: high fever and sepsis. subacute: mild fever, headache, myalgia, weight loss, night sweats. cardiac: murmur, heart failure. splinter hemorrhages: petechial hemorrhages under the fingernails. janeway lesions: small, nontender, erythematous lesions on palms and soles. osler nodes: painful nodules on the pads of fingers and toes. roth spots: retinal hemorrhages.

micro-dx-tx.title: Diagnosis, treatment and prophylaxis
key: Blood cultures are the gold standard: three sets from different venipuncture sites before treatment.
Culture-negative IE: prior antibiotics, fastidious bacteria (Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella, HACEK; confirm by serology or PCR), fungal infection.
Empiric therapy once cultures are drawn: native valve vancomycin + cefepime; prosthetic valve vancomycin + cefepime + gentamicin + rifampin; then targeted therapy.
Prophylaxis before dental or invasive procedures in high-risk clients, 30-60 minutes before: amoxicillin, ampicillin or cefazolin; if penicillin-allergic, a macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline.
micro-dx-tx.text: diagnosis, treatment and prophylaxis organisms shed continuously from the vegetation, so blood cultures catch them, but only if taken before antibiotics. empiric treatment starts right after cultures and is narrowed when results arrive. prophylaxis protects high-risk valves before procedures. a client with a prosthetic valve and penicillin allergy gets azithromycin before a dental extraction. giving the first antibiotic dose before cultures. culture first, cure second. draw three sets of blood cultures from different sites before the first antibiotic. anticipate vancomycin + cefepime for native valves; add gentamicin + rifampin for prosthetic valves. give prophylaxis 30-60 minutes before the procedure; use azithromycin or doxycycline if penicillin-allergic. fastidious organisms in culture-negative ie are confirmed by serology or pcr. blood cultures are the gold standard: three sets from different venipuncture sites before treatment. culture-negative ie: prior antibiotics, fastidious bacteria (coxiella burnetii, bartonella, brucella, hacek; confirm by serology or pcr), fungal infection. empiric therapy once cultures are drawn: native valve vancomycin + cefepime; prosthetic valve vancomycin + cefepime + gentamicin + rifampin; then targeted therapy. prophylaxis before dental or invasive procedures in high-risk clients, 30-60 minutes before: amoxicillin, ampicillin or cefazolin; if penicillin-allergic, a macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline.

micro-lab-id.title: Laboratory identification of IE organisms
key: S. aureus: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; golden yellow colonies, beta hemolysis, ferments mannitol; catalase and coagulase positive.
S. epidermidis: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase positive, coagulase negative.
Viridans streptococci (S. mutans): Gram-positive cocci in chains; alpha hemolysis; optochin resistant; insoluble in bile.
S. pyogenes: Gram-positive cocci in chains; beta hemolysis; catalase negative.
S. pneumoniae: lancet-shaped capsulated diplococci; alpha hemolysis; optochin sensitive; bile soluble.

emb-arches.title: Formation and derivatives of the aortic arches
key: At the 4th week two primitive aortae appear, each with a ventral aorta, a dorsal aorta and a connecting segment; the ventral aortae fuse into the aortic sac with right and left horns.
1st arch: disappears, remnant forms the maxillary arteries. 2nd arch: disappears, remnant forms the stapedial arteries. 5th arch: disappears completely.
3rd arch: proximal parts form the common carotid arteries; distal parts join the dorsal aorta to form the internal carotid arteries. The external carotid is a new bud from the junction.
Left 4th arch: part of the arch of the aorta between the left common carotid and left subclavian. Right 4th arch: proximal part of the right subclavian artery.
6th arch: left proximal forms the left pulmonary artery and left distal forms the ductus arteriosus; right proximal forms the right pulmonary artery and right distal degenerates.
emb-arches.text: formation and derivatives of the aortic arches in the 4th week, paired aortic arch vessels link the aortic sac to the dorsal aortae. some disappear and others are remodeled into the adult great arteries; the recurrent laryngeal nerves hook around the 6th arches, so their adult course depends on which arch segments survive. during pda ligation, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is at risk because it hooks around the ductus. mixing up the 1st (maxillary) and 2nd (stapedial) arch remnants. 1-2 small leftovers, 3 carotid (c is the 3rd letter), 4 systemic (aorta, subclavian), 5 gone, 6 pulmonary. memorize arch by arch: 1 maxillary, 2 stapedial, 3 carotids, 4 aortic arch (left) and right subclavian (right), 5 none, 6 pulmonary arteries and ductus. protect the left recurrent laryngeal nerve during ductus surgery. the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the proximal part of the right subclavian artery. the distal part of the left 6th arch forms the ductus arteriosus. at the 4th week two primitive aortae appear, each with a ventral aorta, a dorsal aorta and a connecting segment; the ventral aortae fuse into the aortic sac with right and left horns. 1st arch: disappears, remnant forms the maxillary arteries. 2nd arch: disappears, remnant forms the stapedial arteries. 5th arch: disappears completely. 3rd arch: proximal parts form the common carotid arteries; distal parts join the dorsal aorta to form the internal carotid arteries. the external carotid is a new bud from the junction. left 4th arch: part of the arch of the aorta between the left common carotid and left subclavian. right 4th arch: proximal part of the right subclavian artery. 6th arch: left proximal forms the left pulmonary artery and left distal forms the ductus arteriosus; right proximal forms the right pulmonary artery and right distal degenerates.

emb-sac-dorsal.title: Aortic sac, dorsal aorta and the origin of the great arteries
key: Aortic sac: arch of the aorta proximal to the brachiocephalic artery. Left horn: arch between the brachiocephalic and left common carotid. Right horn: brachiocephalic artery.
Right dorsal aorta: cranial to the 3rd arch forms the distal internal carotid; at the 7th intersegmental artery forms the distal right subclavian; the rest degenerates.

Left dorsal aorta: at the 7th intersegmental artery forms the subclavian; between the 4th and 6th arches forms the distal arch of the aorta; caudal to the 6th arch forms the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta.
Arch of the aorta from proximal to distal: aortic sac, left horn, left 4th arch, left dorsal aorta between the 4th and 6th arches.
emb-sac-dorsal.text: aortic sac, dorsal aorta and the origin of the great arteries the aortic sac, its horns and the dorsal aortae each contribute a segment to the adult vessels. reading the arch of the aorta from proximal to distal walks through sac, left horn, left 4th arch and left dorsal aorta. a review sheet asks for the origin of the brachiocephalic artery: the right horn of the aortic sac. giving the common carotid to the right horn. right horn = brachiocephalic; left horn = the bit of arch next to it. answer origin questions by locating the segment first: brachiocephalic = right horn; left subclavian = 7th intersegmental artery; right subclavian = right 4th arch + right dorsal aorta at the 7th intersegmental. the common dorsal aorta forms the abdominal aorta and the median sacral artery. aortic sac: arch of the aorta proximal to the brachiocephalic artery. left horn: arch between the brachiocephalic and left common carotid. right horn: brachiocephalic artery. right dorsal aorta: cranial to the 3rd arch forms the distal internal carotid; at the 7th intersegmental artery forms the distal right subclavian; the rest degenerates. left dorsal aorta: at the 7th intersegmental artery forms the subclavian; between the 4th and 6th arches forms the distal arch of the aorta; caudal to the 6th arch forms the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. arch of the aorta from proximal to distal: aortic sac, left horn, left 4th arch, left dorsal aorta between the 4th and 6th arches.

emb-anomalies.title: Anomalies of the aortic arches
key: Patent ductus arteriosus: a patent duct between the left pulmonary artery and the arch of the aorta; associated with aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis and Fallot's tetralogy.
Right arch of aorta: develops from the right dorsal aorta and right 4th arch.
Double arch of aorta: persistence of the distal right dorsal aorta; a vascular ring around the trachea (dyspnea) and esophagus (dysphagia).
Coarctation: constriction of the aorta distal to the left subclavian. Postductal: distal to the ductus, ductus usually closed. Preductal: proximal to the ductus, ductus open.
emb-anomalies.text: anomalies of the aortic arches each anomaly is a normal step that failed: the ductus did not close (pda), the right side persisted instead of the left (right arch), both persisted (double arch, a ring), or a segment narrowed (coarctation). an infant with stridor and feeding difficulty has a vascular ring: double aortic arch. mixing up right arch (one arch on the wrong side) with double arch (two arches). pre-ductal: before the duct, duct open. suspect a double arch in an infant with dyspnea and dysphagia. classify coarctation by where it sits relative to the ductus. a patent ductus connects the left pulmonary artery to the arch of the aorta. patent ductus arteriosus: a patent duct between the left pulmonary artery and the arch of the aorta; associated with aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis and fallot's tetralogy. right arch of aorta: develops from the right dorsal aorta and right 4th arch. double arch of aorta: persistence of the distal right dorsal aorta; a vascular ring around the trachea (dyspnea) and esophagus (dysphagia). coarctation: constriction of the aorta distal to the left subclavian. postductal: distal to the ductus, ductus usually closed. preductal: proximal to the ductus, ductus open.

emb-veins.title: Development of the veins
key: At the 5th week each horn of the sinus venosus receives the umbilical, vitelline and common cardinal veins.
Vitelline veins form the portal and superior mesenteric veins. After birth the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum and the left umbilical vein the ligamentum teres.
Right common cardinal vein: SVC inside the pericardium. Left common cardinal vein: oblique vein of the left atrium.

Right anterior cardinal: SVC outside the pericardium, right brachiocephalic and right internal jugular veins. Left anterior cardinal: left superior intercostal, left brachiocephalic and left internal jugular veins.
Posterior cardinal veins: IVC, common iliac, suprarenal, testicular or ovarian, and renal veins.
emb-veins.text: development of the veins at the 5th week three pairs of veins (umbilical, vitelline, cardinal) drain into the sinus venosus. vitelline veins build the gut's venous drainage, umbilical veins become ligaments after birth, and the cardinal veins become the systemic veins. a nurse traces the ligamentum teres back to the obliterated left umbilical vein. giving the ivc to the vitelline veins. vitelline = viscera; anterior cardinal = above; posterior cardinal = below. sort derivatives by vein: vitelline = portal and smv; anterior cardinal = upper body; posterior cardinal = ivc and lower body veins. the cardinal veins are the main venous drainage of the fetus. at the 5th week each horn of the sinus venosus receives the umbilical, vitelline and common cardinal veins. vitelline veins form the portal and superior mesenteric veins. after birth the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum and the left umbilical vein the ligamentum teres. right common cardinal vein: svc inside the pericardium. left common cardinal vein: oblique vein of the left atrium. right anterior cardinal: svc outside the pericardium, right brachiocephalic and right internal jugular veins. left anterior cardinal: left superior intercostal, left brachiocephalic and left internal jugular veins. posterior cardinal veins: ivc, common iliac, suprarenal, testicular or ovarian, and renal veins.
